::: {#rem-bits-nats}
#### Converting between bits and nats

For any [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $p \in (0, 1]$,
the change-of-base rule for [logarithms](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-logarithm) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\log_2 p
&= \frac{-\ln p}{\ln 2}\\
&\approx 1.443 \times (-\ln p).
\end{aligned}
$$

So a [value](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-realization) with a [surprisal](#def-surprisal) of $1$ [nat](#def-nat) has a surprisal of
$1 / \ln 2 \approx 1.443$ [bits](#def-bit),
and the $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$ [nats](#def-nat) of @exm-coin-nats
are exactly $\ln 2 / \ln 2 = 1$ [bit](#def-bit).

A bit as a unit of information is not the same thing as
a bit as a binary digit.
The name [shannon](#def-bit) refers only to the unit of information,
so it avoids this ambiguity.
A binary digit whose two values are equally likely
has a surprisal of exactly $1$ bit, whichever value it takes.
A binary digit that is $0$ nine times in ten does not:
the value $0$ has a surprisal of $-\log_2 0.9 \approx 0.152$ bits,
and the value $1$ has a surprisal of $-\log_2 0.1 \approx 3.322$ bits.

:::
